title: John Smeaton's lighthouse copied the shape of an oak tree and lit its reef for 122 years

cover.alt: Smeaton's Tower, a red-and-white striped stone lighthouse with a flared base, standing on the grass of Plymouth Hoe above the sea.

body: The Eddystone reef off Plymouth wrecked the first two lighthouses built on it: a storm swept away one in 1703 and fire destroyed the next in 1755. In 1756 **John Smeaton**, a mathematical instrument maker and aspiring civil engineer, proposed a stone tower **modelled on the shape of an oak tree**, broad and heavy at the base and narrowing towards the top. He locked its granite blocks together with dovetail joints and marble dowels, and pioneered *hydraulic lime*, a concrete that sets underwater. First lit on 16 October 1759, it worked until 1882, when erosion of the rock beneath it made it shake in big waves.

slides.alt: A tall grey granite lighthouse rising from the sea, with a short, dark stone stump topped by a thin mast beside it.
slides.caption: Today's Eddystone lighthouse, on a reef off Plymouth, with the stump of Smeaton's tower beside it. Its upper part was taken down and rebuilt on Plymouth Hoe.

slides.heading: Eddystone's lighthouses, oldest first
slides.explanation: First lit in 1698, 1708, 1759 and 1882. Douglass's tower is still in use.

slides.heading: How long each lighthouse worked
slides.note: Years from first lighting to loss or retirement, rounded down; Douglass's figure is as of 2026.

slides.heading: Built like a jigsaw
slides.text: Cornish granite formed the foundations and the outside, with lighter Portland limestone inside. Each block was cut to dovetail into its neighbours and was pinned in place with marble dowels.

slides.label: tallow candles lit Smeaton's lantern
slides.text: They hung in a chandelier at the top of the 18 m tower, which was 7.9 m across at the base and 5.2 m at the top.

slides.heading: The two that came before
slides.text: Henry Winstanley's lighthouse was destroyed in the Great Storm of 1703, killing him and five others. John Rudyard's burned in December 1755; its keeper, 94-year-old Henry Hall, died several days later after swallowing molten lead from the lantern roof.

slides.question: Why was Smeaton's lighthouse replaced?
options: The rock under it was eroding
slides.explanation: Erosion under the tower made it shake from side to side when large waves hit. The original base still stands on the rock, 37 m from the new lighthouse.
